extracted.intended_audience: DHS/USCIS rulewriters and regulators; administrative law reviewers; stakeholders preparing notice-and-comment submissions (states, advocates, health and safety agencies).
extracted.subtask_description: A formal multi-state legal objection to DHS/USCIS’s proposed public charge rule (NPRM) identifying legal, procedural, and policy standards the agency must satisfy when changing longstanding public-charge policy. Intended to guide agency rulemaking and inform public comments and litigation strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/settled meaning of 'public charge'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Public charge' historically means an individual with the inherent inability to be self-supporting or someone 'primarily dependent on the government for subsistence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency rulemaking must respect the well-settled, century-long judicial and administrative interpretation that 'public charge' targets persons likely to be long-term dependents, not immigrants who receive some supplemental assistance. The Proposed Rule's expansive redefinition is inconsistent with precedent (e.g., Matter of Harutunian; numerous circuit decisions) and with Congress's reenactments in 1952 and 1996.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow definition of 'public cash assistance'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the 2022 Rule, 'public cash assistance' is limited solely to Supplemental Security Income (SSI), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF), or other 'cash benefit programs for income maintenance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rules should retain or adopt a narrow cash-only definition (SSI/TANF/other income-maintenance programs) and not treat routine non-cash programs as cash assistance. Deleting this limitation would expand inadmissibility beyond historical bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude non-cash benefits from public-charge consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-cash benefits (e.g., SNAP, CHIP, most Medicaid, Section 8 housing assistance, public housing) should not be considered in public-charge determinations (except Medicaid when it is government-paid long-term institutionalization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must not treat common supplemental benefits—designed to promote health and mobility—as indicators of future public charge. The Proposed Rule's inclusion of such benefits would penalize routine, low-dollar supports and contradicts the 1999 Guidance and the 2022 Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances test with no sole-factor rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Public-charge determinations should apply a totality-of-the-circumstances test where 'the existence or absence of a particular factor should never be the sole criterion' for finding someone likely to become a public charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain explicit regulatory language that no single factor is dispositive. Provide examples of how multiple factors are weighed to avoid arbitrary conclusions and ensure consistent application across officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear definition of 'receipt' of benefits (beneficiary-based; application not receipt)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether someone 'has received' a benefit should hinge on whether that person is a listed beneficiary of the benefit; mere application for a benefit should not constitute receipt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should specify that only actual receipt as a listed beneficiary counts for public-charge analysis; mere application or outreach should not be treated as receipt. This prevents penalizing innocuous or unsuccessful applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify treatment of household/family members' benefit use
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule must explain whether and how benefits used by other household members (including U.S. citizen children or other exempt relatives) will be treated in an applicant's public-charge determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit standards and guardrails (or categorical rules) to prevent immigration officers from counting lawful benefits obtained by other household members against an applicant. Avoid using household-level data as a proxy for individual inadmissibility without defined limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect prior lawful benefit use from retroactive penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: A final rule should not retroactively penalize residents for past lawful receipt of benefits that were permitted under prior policy/regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency must state explicitly that prior lawful benefit use—especially use relied upon under prior rules—will not be used to find someone a public charge. Failure to protect reliance interests risks arbitrary and capricious action and likely legal challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient public comment period and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Thirty days for public comment is inadequate for a rule of this magnitude and complexity; stakeholders need more time to identify impacts and submit evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extend the notice-and-comment period to allow comprehensive analysis of legal, fiscal, and public-health impacts and meaningful participation from states, providers, and affected communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasoned explanation for change and consideration of reliance interests (APA compliance)
rubrics_metrics.description: When rescinding longstanding regulations (e.g., the 2022 Rule), the agency must supply a reasoned analysis for the change, acknowledge and evaluate reliance interests, and consider alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comply with Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Assn. v. State Farm, Regents v. DHS, FCC v. Fox: identify reliance interests created by prior rules, analyze how they arose, and weigh reasonable alternatives; failure to do so renders a change arbitrary and capricious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute sub-regulatory guidance for formal rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing the rescinded rule with sub-regulatory 'guidance' without notice-and-comment would improperly deny the public participation required by the APA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency intends to create policy that has direct effects on rights/obligations, it must use formal rulemaking. Interpretive or policy statements cannot serve as a substitute for rules that materially affect stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantify and analyze fiscal, administrative, and public-health impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must meaningfully analyze costs: reductions in federal transfer payments, increased uncompensated care, state budget impacts, IT/training/reprogramming costs, and downstream public-health consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide state- and program-level estimates, account for prior evidence (e.g., impacts from the 2019 Rule), and consider non-federal cost-shifting (e.g., to hospitals, local programs, food banks) rather than treating 'reductions in transfer payments' as benign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with controlling case law and administrative precedents
rubrics_metrics.description: A lawful rule must grapple with appellate courts' analyses that found the 2019 Rule likely unlawful and must not cherry-pick authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address and distinguish Second, Seventh, Ninth Circuit reasoning (and related district-court findings), explain departures if any, and show why proposed interpretations are consistent with statute and precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerate minimum statutory factors (IIRIRA) and explain weighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress specified that public-charge determinations should consider at minimum: age, health, family status, assets/resources/financial status, and education and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit how these factors will be evaluated and weighted in individualized determinations to provide predictability and reduce arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restore or define explicit categories/exemptions (e.g., refugees, asylees, humanitarian classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should explicitly identify who is not subject to public-charge determinations and preserve longstanding exemptions (e.g., refugees, asylees, T- and U-visa holders, special juvenile immigrants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reinstate clear regulatory text (e.g., §§ 212.20–212.23) or equivalent explicit protections so individuals who relied on exemptions are not placed in uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear limits/guardrails to constrain officer discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rule's deletion of definitions and its invitation to consider 'any type of public benefits' would vest unbounded discretion in individual officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt enumerated, limiting language or decision rules to prevent inconsistent, arbitrary, or absurd outcomes (e.g., clarifying that widely available services such as policing or sanitation cannot be counted). Provide training and publicly available interpretive tools subject to notice-and-comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify interaction with other statutes (PRWORA, affidavit-of-support, Medicaid emergency exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency must explain how PRWORA, affidavit-of-support requirements, and other statutes (e.g., Medicaid emergency-treatment exception) relate to public-charge determinations; PRWORA does not itself alter the INA meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on PRWORA or affidavit-of-support provisions as a basis to expand public-charge scope without legal justification. Clarify that emergency Medicaid and statutorily preserved state programs will not be used to find inadmissibility.
